There is a particular kind of quiet that only exists in the hour before dawn, when the streetlights still burn but the windows have started to lighten at their edges. I find myself drawn to that hour. It belongs to no one in particular. The bakers are already up, the early joggers haven't yet come out, and the city hasn't decided what kind of day it will be.

I think a lot about attention, about how it is the one thing we truly spend. Money can be earned back and time can be reorganized, but a moment of full attention, once given away, is gone. We scatter it across notifications and half-listened conversations, and then wonder why the days feel thin. Yet when attention does land fully on something, a cup of coffee going cold while you watch steam curl upward, or a child explaining a drawing with great seriousness, the world briefly becomes dense and vivid again.

Maybe that is why I like the early morning. It asks very little. It simply offers a clean stretch of time before the noise arrives, and if you sit still long enough, you start to notice things: the way a sparrow hops along a gutter as though it has somewhere important to be, the faint hum of a refrigerator in the next room, the slow change in color as the sky moves from gray to pale blue.

None of these things are remarkable on their own. But together they make a kind of argument for slowing down. The world is rarely as loud as we assume. It mostly waits for us to notice it, and it is generous with its details to anyone willing to look.
